item.title: China opens trade shortcut to SE Asia
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
China opens trade shortcut to SE Asia Pinglu Canal expected to drive further opening-up of western region China opened a vital waterway on Wednesday, giving its landlocked southwestern areas a shortcut to the coast and overseas markets, as the country moves to further strengthen its trade relations with regional neighbors, particularly those in Southeast Asia. The Pinglu Canal, built in the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region at a cost of 72.7 billion yuan ($10.8 billion), stretches for 134.2 kilometers from the Xijin reservoir in the county-level city of Hengzhou to the Qinzhou Port in the Beibu Gulf. It is the first waterway built in the country to connect a river system directly to the sea since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949. The canal shortens the inland waterway journeys of goods from southwestern China by more than 560 km compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong province. It is expected to reduce overall logistics expenses and save more than 5 billion yuan in transportation costs each year. Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang, who attended the canal's opening ceremony, called for making full use of the new waterway to develop a first-class international gateway port in the Beibu Gulf and support further opening-up of China's western region. Ding also called for efficient operation of the canal, which serves as key infrastructure for multimodal transportation integrating river, rail and sea, and is a backbone project of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor — a strategic route connecting China's inland areas with regional and global markets. Construction of the Pinglu Canal started in August 2022 to address a long-standing geographical problem in terms of trade. While Guangxi boasts a coastline and borders Vietnam, its major inland rivers flow east, which means cargo moving by water from Nanning, the capital of Guangxi, and other parts of the Xijiang River basin could only reach the sea through Guangdong. The Pinglu Canal, designed to handle vessels of the 5,000-metric-ton class, now allows cargo to turn south and reach the Beibu Gulf — the closest maritime outlet for much of southwestern China — through the Qinzhou Port. One of the biggest engineering challenges during construction of the canal was navigating a difference of 65 meters in the water level between its northern end and the sea. Three navigation hubs — Madao, Qishi and Qingnian — featuring twin-line ship locks were built to raise and lower vessels, effectively acting as giant elevators. Ni Yuping, vice-dean of Tsinghua University's School of Humanities in Beijing, placed the megaproject in a broader context, saying that one of the key questions it seeks to answer is "how western China can better integrate into the global economy". Unlike the Suez Canal and the Panama Canal, which primarily provide shortcuts for vessels between major seas and oceans, the Pinglu Canal gives a vast inland economic hinterland a shorter route to the coast — and from there to international markets. Wu Tao, a history professor at Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong, noted that inland waterway shipping routes "remain irreplaceable" even though China's road, rail and air transportation networks have expanded. Their large carrying capacity and relatively low logistics costs make inland waterways particularly suited for bulk cargo, Wu said. For businesses, the new canal is already dictating logistics and investment decisions. On Sept 8, a consignment of auto parts from Chinese vehicle manufacturer SAIC-GM-Wuling left Liuzhou for Nanning Port, before continuing by ship through the Pinglu Canal to reach Can Tho Port in Vietnam. The company said the new river-sea route could cut its logistics costs by about 10 percent. "For us, the freight saved is real profit, and that translates directly into greater price competitiveness in ASEAN and other global markets," said Cai Yan, a senior technical officer at SAIC-GM-Wuling. The canal has added waterway to the company's existing road and rail transportation options, giving it more flexibility as it expands its business and production links across Southeast Asia, Cai said. The new route is being factored into investment plans of companies. About 50 km from the Pinglu Canal's northern end, French chemicals producer SNF Group is building a plant in Nanning's Liujing Industrial Park, with an annual capacity of 370,000 tons. The factory, which will be the group's largest production base in southern China, is expected to start operations in stages before June 2027. "The Pinglu Canal will reduce our logistics costs and enable convenient delivery to South China and all of Southeast Asia. It offers great advantages in both materials sourcing and product distribution," said Thomas Wilsius, head of the company's Nanning project. The waterway is likely to bring more Southeast Asian products to the Chinese market. Philippine Ambassador to China Jaime A. FlorCruz, who visited the canal with a group of ASEAN envoys in July, said that fresh seafood and other time-sensitive products could be exported more efficiently from his country to China. "In the long run, this will benefit not only the local people, but the broader region and even the world," he said, adding that shorter shipping distances, lower freight costs and faster deliveries would bring tangible benefits to fishermen, farmers, traders and entrepreneurs. For Shen Guiping, a resident of Shangjing village in Qinzhou, who took part in relocation work for the project, the opening of the Pinglu Canal carries a more personal meaning. "It almost feels like a dream that has finally been realized. It is something generations of locals hoped for," she said. Contact the writers at luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: AI production's prime-time triumph
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
What happens when an AI-generated series debuts on prime-time TV? A ratings win, a regulatory breakthrough, and a gold rush in the A-share market — Chinese yuan-denominated stocks listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges. Recently, the mythology-themed series Beyond Wukong made history as the first AI-produced long-form drama to secure a prime-time slot on a major television network — Hunan Satellite TV. The premiere immediately topped the ratings among all provincial satellite channels in the same time slot. The production is also the first to clear the country's review-while-airing mechanism — a fast-track approval process introduced last August under the National Radio and Television Administration's 21 reform measures, designed to diversify and accelerate content supply for major TV platforms. Only the first five episodes have been released so far, with the remaining episodes to be produced, submitted for review, and rolled out progressively as the broadcast continues. Since the premiere on Aug 31, Mango Excellent Media Co, the show's producer, has seen its A-share stock surge by the daily 20 percent limit on two consecutive trading days. By the close of trading on Sept 4 — the same day the fifth episode aired — the share price had jumped from 14.15 yuan on Aug 28 to 21.25 yuan, adding over 10 billion yuan ($1.5 billion) in market capitalization in less than a week. Except for the numbers, Beyond Wukong has ignited a broader public conversation about the evolving relationship between AI and the art of visual storytelling. For Li Dongshen, the series director, the implications are both personal and profound. Previously a documentary filmmaker, Li says directing this AI-generated series has shifted his perception of what he produces — from "artworks" to "visual products". He notes that each 40-minute episode costs approximately 900,000 yuan to produce, or about 20,000 to 30,000 yuan per minute — less than one-tenth the per-minute production cost of an animated film of mediocre quality. In his view, the traditional film and television industry has been built around the camera for 150 years: writers author scenes, art directors re-create them, lighting technicians set the lights, cinematographers record the footage, editors assemble the final cut, and directors coordinate every department along the way. The production of Beyond Wukong, however, has completely abandoned this camera-centric mindset and established an entirely new production logic. "You have to remove the camera from your mind," he says. The underlying logic of AIGC (AI-generated content) video is frame-by-frame generation — essentially a sequence of temporally consistent individual images stitched together. "You have to think clearly about who is in each frame, where they are, which direction the light is coming from, and what emotional beat the scene is hitting. Then leave the transitions between frames to the model." The production team behind Beyond Wukong has more than 100 members, 70 percent of whom come from art-related backgrounds. Li believes that for future creators working with AIGC in film and television, the two most essential qualities are imagination, namely the ability to envision countless key frames, and judgment, since AI models can generate dozens of possibilities at once and creators need to select the best one quickly. Putting this philosophy into practice, however, is no easy feat. During the early stage of working with AI models such as Seedance 2.0 and Seedance 2.5, prompts for a single shot could run up to 7,000 to 8,000 Chinese characters, with granular details specifying which muscle on a character's face should begin to twitch. "So far, there hasn't been a single scene we could imagine that AI was unable to generate. The real problem right now is that our imagination can't keep up with what the models are capable of," Li says. "Within a year at the earliest, or two years at a conservative estimate, more than 90 percent of all film and television productions will incorporate AIGC to some extent," predicts Li. Beyond Wukong is adapted from an anonymous mythological novel from the late Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), and serves as a sequel to the classic Journey to the West. It follows the descendants of the original pilgrimage crew as they reunite and journey once more to the Western Heaven in search of the definitive interpretation of the scriptures. Ren Xu, general manager of Mango Excellent Media's AIGC Innovation Content Center, explains why the company chose this work as its AIGC pilot. In an era of exploding AI-generated content and shrinking audience attention, a familiar story tied to Journey to the West lowers the barrier to market entry, while adapting the sequel rather than the original allows far greater creative freedom. "Technically, a mythological theme also gives AI-generated content a margin for error, while its grand world-building and fantastical settings maximize AIGC's visual strengths," he adds. Ren notes that while AIGC has dramatically lowered barriers to content creation, triggering an explosion of AI-produced short dramas, only a handful can be considered truly high-quality. For the industry to evolve from "experimental works" to "consistent quality production", it must crack the challenge of long-form consistency. "One major bottleneck is maintaining visual uniformity across dozens of episodes. A character's face might change in the next shot, and costumes, movements, and environments are prone to distortion — all magnified in a long series," he says. Ren maintains that Beyond Wukong has pioneered an industrialized production workflow tailored to AIGC. The company built an end-to-end, AI-powered pipeline on its proprietary platform, LumeCreate, spanning everything from character design and storyboarding to final rendering and post-production. "This proves that AIGC long-form production can move from a 'handicraft workshop' to an 'industrial assembly line'," he says. The 109 character assets and 143 scene assets can be reused in future episodes and shared across other mythology projects, enabling long-term IP management and value growth, Ren adds. In response to viewer feedback that the pacing is sometimes slow, Li says they will make adjustments in subsequent productions of the seasonal series. "We haven't finished writing all the episodes for the first season yet, so that the story direction can be co-created with the audience. If I find that viewers have proposed a very interesting storyline, I will definitely adjust the one I currently have in mind," Li explains. Following the pilot, the company has charted a clear AIGC roadmap targeting three areas: children's animation, revival of classic Chinese-style IP, and quality mid-to-long-form dramas for female audiences, covering both serialized and stand-alone content.

item.title: HK to target breakthroughs in core tech
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
Hong Kong to target breakthroughs in core tech Hong Kong will step up efforts to develop into an international innovation and technology center, targeting breakthroughs in core technologies such as artificial intelligence and life sciences, with the push backed by modern finance, expanded public research platforms and closer collaboration with the Chinese mainland. The policy direction and specific measures outlined in the city's latest development blueprints will help strengthen Hong Kong's innovation and technology ecosystem and accelerate the commercialization of research outcomes, industry insiders said. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Wednesday, while delivering the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2026-2030), that Hong Kong will continue to increase its expenditure on innovation activities as a share of gross domestic product, aiming to raise the ratio to 3 percent after 2030, from about 1.63 percent in 2024. Lee said the Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund is expected to be launched this year, covering five thematic sectors, including life and health technology, AI and robotics. With a HK$10 billion ($1.27 billion) injection from the HKSAR government and market contributions at a ratio of 1 to at least 3, the fund is projected to reach at least HK$40 billion in total. In his annual Policy Address released on the same day, Lee provided further details, saying that about 20 fund managers have been preliminarily shortlisted to raise capital for the establishment of sub-funds. The two road maps also proposed advancing the development of the "three major innovation and technology parks and five key research and development institutions". The latter include the Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute, which is expected to begin operation this year, and the Life and Health Technology Research Institute. Preparatory work for the LHTRI, which will focus on "AI + life sciences", will be largely completed by the end of the year. "We will basically have established an international innovation and technology center based in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, serving the entire country and connected to the world, after 2030," Lee said. He added that this will give rise to a new paradigm for innovation and technology development, with enterprises as the key players, unicorns taking the lead, and modern finance empowering the integrated development of technological and industrial innovation. Joseph Chan, associate director of the Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship at the Business School of the University of Hong Kong, said the "finance+" strategy is a smart move because it treats finance as an essential engine powering technological innovation, rather than as an isolated sector. Innovation and technology are increasingly becoming key drivers of Hong Kong's economy, with their contributions reflected in a growing share of the city's GDP, Chan said. "The HKSAR government has both the will and a concrete plan," he said, citing the Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund and major research institutions as examples of policy support. "In doing so, far greater social resources can be rallied, and more importantly, (this can) generate impactful outcomes that benefit both the people's livelihoods and the wider national economy." Speaking of the "three major innovation and technology parks", which include the Hong Kong Park of the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone, Hannah Jeong, head of valuation and advisory services at CBRE Hong Kong, said the coordinated development model is expected to create a more comprehensive innovation ecosystem supporting research, commercialization and advanced manufacturing. Jeong said that while physical infrastructure is important, "a key success factor will be Hong Kong's ability to attract leading international technology companies, research institutes and universities". Commenting on the proposed Hong Kong Innovation and Technology Application Scenario Promotion Centre and the target of establishing the SAR's first national manufacturing innovation center by 2027, Victor Kwok, deputy research director of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said the two institutions will play complementary roles in building the ecosystem. The application scenario center will help accelerate the process of moving innovation solutions from the R&D stage to market validation and implementation, Kwok said. The national manufacturing innovation center, meanwhile, can help overcome bottlenecks in key technologies and promote the industrialization of research outcomes. "Together, the two institutions will help address Hong Kong's long-standing weakness in midstream and downstream commercialization in its innovation and technology ecosystem," he added. irisli@chinadailyhk.com

item.title: Domestic firms score with AI tennis technologies
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-17
Andre Agassi once famously branded fellow tennis great Pete Sampras "robotic" for his metronomic serve and emotionless on-court demeanor, but who knows what the eight-time Grand Slam winner would think of China's latest high-tech breakthrough. On a tennis court in Bao'an district of Shenzhen, Guangdong province's tech hub, a player can now scan a QR code, open a shared equipment locker and wheel out a robot to practice against. When a ball is struck, cameras track the ball's trajectory, and the robot scurries along the baseline, catches the ball and fires another one back from its new position. Chinese technology companies are developing artificial intelligence-powered sports equipment to create these training partners, which never tire and are always available. Unlike traditional ball machines that remain fixed in one corner and feed balls in preset patterns, some of the new machines can move left, right, forward and backward, varying the launch point to test players' footwork and reactions more effectively. Shenzhen-based Acemate's robot uses cameras to track the ball and the player, and can move across the court. A catching net collects an incoming shot before the robot launches the next ball, making the session feel more like a rally than a repetitive feeding drill. The product has attracted attention overseas. At a trial event in New York, more than 200 tennis enthusiasts lined up to try out the Chinese robot, according to the company. Acemate launched its mobile tennis robot on an overseas crowdfunding platform in May 2025, and has shipped about 6,000 units to over 60 countries and regions, with overseas markets accounting for more than 70 percent of sales, according to Huang Zihui, the company's CEO. "It is no longer simply about 'Made in China'," Huang said. "Chinese companies are defining new product categories and taking them to the global market." Shenzhen has also begun piloting shared rentals of AI tennis robots this year, with some machines available for about 88 yuan ($12) an hour. For players like Wang Yinan, the appeal is simple. Wang, who plays four or five times a week, said finding suitable partners in Shenzhen became increasingly difficult after he reached the 2.5-to-3.0 level on the National Tennis Rating Program scale. That range represents advanced-beginner to lower-intermediate recreational players. With a robot, "whenever I have time, I can come and play", he said. AceiiLab, founded in Shenzhen in late 2024, has deliberately chosen not to make its first robot catch every returning ball. Instead, its A1 robot uses a proprietary binocular vision system to track the player, ball position, speed and trajectory, and can move at up to 5 meters per second while feeding balls from different locations around the court. "Tennis is fundamentally about judging rhythm and spatial position," said Chao Guang, co-founder of AceiiLab. "Trying to catch every shot could interrupt the feeding rhythm, demand more computing power and heavier hardware, and push up costs for users." According to the General Administration of Sport of China, about 25.36 million people played tennis in China in 2025, with participation expected to top 32 million by 2030. Shanghai-based Future Mind is also going after the same fast-growing market. Founder and CEO Zhang Haibo said the company has sold more than 100,000 units of products cumulatively, and that sales in the first half of the year were considerably higher year-on-year. More than 90 percent of customers are individual consumers, he added. Zhang said that he expects AI-powered sports products to become standard equipment at tennis courts around the world within the next two to three years. He estimated that current penetration is only about 3 to 4 percent, but sees it climbing to between 30 and 40 percent over that period.

item.title: High-tech sector lifts industrial growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
High-tech sector lifts industrial growth China's economy drew strong support from new growth drivers in August, with double-digit growth in high-tech manufacturing and solid external demand underpinning fast industrial growth, officials and experts said on Tuesday. However, the transition from old to new growth drivers remains marked by structural divergence, they cautioned, adding that a more proactive policy response is needed to revive domestic demand after a second straight month of slower retail sales growth and a deepening contraction in fixed-asset investment. Their remarks came on the heels of fresh data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Tuesday showing that the country's industrial output rose 5.2 percent year-on-year in August, accelerating from a 4.5 percent increase in July. According to Fu Linghui, the bureau's spokesman and chief economist, the strong performance was underpinned mainly by new growth drivers, which accounted for over 60 percent of industrial output growth. High-tech and digital product manufacturing, for example, grew 16.7 percent and 15.7 percent year-on-year, respectively. "The bright spot remains industrial activity," said Lynn Song, chief economist for China at Dutch bank ING, pointing to resilient external demand and China's continued technological and industrial upgrading. That upgrading is taking China beyond its traditional strengths in low-cost, large-scale manufacturing toward "ecosystem and innovation leadership", US investment bank Morgan Stanley said in a recent report. The report projected that the transition could raise the country's potential GDP level by about 3.5 percent by 2035 and lift its share of global manufacturing value-add from around 28 percent to 30 percent. The growing role of new growth drivers was also evident in investment, with spending in high-tech industries rising 5.2 percent year-on-year in the first eight months. "The investment mix in manufacturing is improving," said Wang Qing, chief macroeconomic analyst at Orient Golden Credit Rating International. Also, the services sector is shifting toward more technology-intensive activities, with information transmission, software and information technology services contributing more than one-fifth of overall growth in services production in August, the NBS said. In contrast to the strong performance of emerging sectors, weak domestic demand continued to weigh on the broader economy, with consumption growth moderating and the contraction in investment deepening, analysts said. Retail sales, a key gauge of consumption, rose 0.4 percent year-on-year in August, slowing from 0.6 percent in July, while fixed-asset investment fell 7.2 percent year-on-year in the first eight months, compared with a 6.7 percent decline in the January-July period, the NBS said. "New growth drivers have yet to fully offset the weakening of traditional ones," said Luo Zhiheng, chief economist and head of the research institute at Yuekai Securities, calling for quicker issuance of special-purpose bonds and accelerated fiscal spending. Experts said ample policy room is still available, additional measures — including interest rate and reserve requirement ratio cuts, and further issuance of government bonds — are expected to help strengthen growth momentum toward the year-end. Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said policy support is strengthening and implementation is accelerating, noting the recent recapitalization plans totaling up to 360 billion yuan ($53.6 billion) for State-owned financial institutions. New policy-based financial instruments totaling 800 billion yuan began rolling out in early September, with funding expected to be deployed mainly in September and October, Wen added. Echoing that view, Sheana Yue, a senior economist at British think tank Oxford Economics, said: "Accelerated bond issuance and policy-bank financing are likely to eventually boost government investment." On the monetary front, Wang of Orient Golden Credit Rating International said the central bank could cut interest rates by 10 basis points and the reserve requirement ratio by 0.5 percentage point around the end of the third quarter. Such easing would help boost consumption, stabilize investment and support the property market, he said.

item.title: Good chicken keeps its flavor with just a peck of seasoning
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
"No chicken, no feast." The saying still holds true in Guangdong province, where poultry remains a fixture on family tables and banquet menus, while some local specialties are finding new fans beyond the dining table. At LN Dongfang Hotel in Guangzhou, the provincial capital, Shishi chicken has been prepared for 65 years. From Fengkai county in western Guangdong, Xinghua chickens are shipped across China, with their eggs also sought by pastry chefs. Yet as the way that chicken is produced, served and consumed changes, one standard remains: The chicken itself should taste like chicken. "That is the highest praise Guangzhou diners can give," said Lu Jianrong, executive chef at Yanlegong, a restaurant at the hotel. The aim is chicken that is tender yet firm, with a fresh, savory flavor that is not masked by seasoning, Lu said. This emphasis on natural flavor has shaped Guangdong's rich tradition of chicken dishes and local breeds. One example is Shishi chicken, a traditional Guangzhou dish created in the early 20th century at Xinji, a Cantonese restaurant on what is now Beijing Road. It was named after the nearby Guangzhou Municipal Normal School, known as "Shishi". For Lu, it starts with the bird itself. The restaurant uses chickens aged 160 to 180 days. "Only a chicken that has been raised for long enough can develop the right flavor," Lu said. The key cooking method is slow-poaching rather than plain boiling. The chicken is cooked in stock, kept at about 85 C, that is made with ingredients including ham, shrimp, dried scallops, squid, ginger and scallions. A technique known as "three lifts and three dips" helps to regulate the temperature and cook the chicken evenly. "If the water is too hot, the skin can split and the meat can become tough; if it is too cool, the chicken may not cook properly," Lu said. Knowing when it is done also takes experience. Chefs feel the leg joint to judge doneness, rather than relying solely on a timer. "Machines can measure temperature, but every chicken is different in size and texture," Lu said. "The final judgment still requires a chef to make adjustments based on the individual bird." Once cooked, the chicken is quickly cooled in chilled stock, then cut into pieces and finished with roasted peanut oil and a savory soy-based sauce. "The sauce is there to enhance the chicken's flavor, not to cover it up," Lu said. The same preference for freshness and natural flavor can be found in Guangdong's local breeds. Xinghua chicken, from Fengkai county, is a national geographical indication product known for its small size, thin skin and tender meat. Locals describe it as having "glass-like skin and crisp, delicate bones". Chen Yanying, who runs a restaurant specializing in dishes made with Xinghua chicken, said the restaurant works with local farms to maintain a steady supply. The breed is also finding new uses beyond the dining table. Its eggs are being made into cakes, pastries and egg pancakes, while the restaurant's partner farms sell about 2 million birds a year, with the majority shipped beyond Guangdong. Poached Xinghua chicken is among the most popular preparations. The chicken is repeatedly lifted from hot water, briefly cooled and returned to the pot. The method produces crisp skin and tender meat, with a gelatinous layer forming between the skin and flesh. In Fengkai, it is commonly served with ginger-and-scallion soy sauce, while Guangzhou diners often pair it with minced ginger and peanut oil. For visitors to Guangdong, especially those trying Cantonese cuisine for the first time, local chicken offers a straightforward introduction to the region's culinary philosophy — start with the ingredient and let the cooking reveal its natural qualities. Though the preparations differ, the principle is the same: Seasoning should complement the ingredient rather than overwhelm it. "Cantonese cuisine emphasizes freshness, lightness, crispness, tenderness and smoothness," Lu said. "With good ingredients, you don't need too many complicated seasonings. The key is to bring out their natural flavor." Zheng Caixiong in Guangzhou contributed to this story.

item.title: Heilongjiang leverages black soil culture
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
Heilongjiang leverages black soil culture Fertile paddies in NE China, customized experience making rice a true cash crop As the country's "granary", Northeast China's Heilongjiang province has continuously produced high-quality grains, laying a solid foundation for national food security. In recent years, the province has actively explored new paths for agricultural transformation and upgrading as consumers begin to place greater importance on food traceability, production involvement and rural cultural experiences. The province is vigorously developing customized agricultural models such as paddy field adoption and exclusive order-based planting, shifting consumer demand to the forefront of field production and giving end-users a more personal, hands-on experience with the staple grain. By integrating immersive cultural and tourism scenarios like paddy field sightseeing, agricultural study tours and intangible cultural heritage harvest festivals, the strategy marks a shift in the rice cultivation sector from merely selling products to selling experiences and culture. In Wuchang, Harbin, through its rice field adoption and custom farming programs, Qiaofu Dayuan Agricultural Co Ltd draws on the city's intangible cultural heritage of agricultural festivals, creating an immersive rice farming study system, said Wang Dan, administrative manager of the company. The company manages 250,000 mu (16,667 hectares) of rice fields at the core production area of Wuchang rice, which is famous for its unique flavor and texture, and is grown in traditional Northeast China black soil known for its highly fertile characteristics. The company has innovatively introduced a personalized model based on square meters, launching an annual family package for 100-sq m rice paddies, offering services including freshly milled rice delivery and farming experiences, Wang said. In 2026, the company achieved high-end rice field adoption of 3,333 hectares, with contracted sales of 195 million yuan ($29 million), and group client customization of 8,666 hectares, with contracted sales of 890 million yuan. Through standardized planting, diversified customization and full-chain services, the company continues to enhance the golden brand of customized agriculture centered on Wuchang rice. Lots of adoption clients have visited their adopted rice fields to participate in festival activities and experience the joys and challenges of harvesting. The park is equipped with a rice culture museum, sightseeing trails, specialty homestays and rice field photo spots, transforming rice production into a new agricultural, cultural and tourism business model integrating sightseeing, study, experience, aesthetics and consumption. For 11 consecutive years, the company has held agricultural festivals such as the Rice Planting Festival, Rice Flower Festival and Rice Harvest Festival. In 2024, the company established the Rice Countryside Town Study Base, creating a comprehensive study project integrating rice science popularization, farming practices and cultural experiences. The study courses cover visits to the rice culture museum, rice growth science education, hands-on farming experiences like planting and harvesting, rice processing observation and understanding the rice-duck symbiosis ecosystem. Visitors can enter the fields to experience farming and harvesting, to understand "every grain comes from hard work", while learning about the historical origins of Wuchang rice and the mystique of black soil farming culture.

item.title: Fahai Temple murals: 'Naked-eye 3D' from 500 years ago
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
Mural painting is where painting began. Chinese murals, with their long and distinguished tradition, unfold like a history of painting written across walls. Alina Efimova, a cultural observer from Russia with a deep interest in Chinese murals, sat down with Dong Zhuo, vice dean of the School of Restoration at the Central Academy of Fine Arts, for a cross-cultural conversation. Amid the vast and dazzling array of Chinese murals, what makes the murals of Fahai Temple so exceptionally refined? Why do netizens describe them as having a "naked-eye 3D" quality? And where does that faint halo of light come from? Follow their conversation to take in the grandeur and exquisite beauty of the Fahai Temple murals — a masterpiece of imperial mural painting from the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644). Into Chinese Art is an immersive cultural interview series produced by China Daily Culture Channel, where international hosts engage with art experts through interactive discussions, offering audiences a deeper understanding of Chinese art and aesthetics. The fourth season of Into Chinese Art focuses on murals.

item.title: China's message of peace to the world
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
China's message of peace to the world Share - WeChat
Join China Daily reporter Zhao Manfeng at the 13th Beijing Xiangshan Forum, where experts and officials called for greater trust, dialogue and cooperation amid growing uncertainties in the international environment. Over the 20 years since its founding, the Beijing Xiangshan Forum has played an important role in building consensus on security, promoting defense cooperation and safeguarding regional peace and stability. Themed "Build Consensus on Stability, Advance Security Governance Together," this year's forum has brought together about 2,000 guests, including government officials, experts, scholars, and observers from more than 100 countries, regions, and international organizations.
